html:
A masquerade of the Yoruba of southeastern Benin, southwestern Nigeria and Togo, performed to honour and please "our mothers", the elder women and the mystical power they are believed to hold.

Men wear carved wooden headdresses, often showing scenes of daily life or satire, with women's clothing, and dance to drums at festivals after harvest or in times of trouble. It probably began in the Ketu region in the 18th century. UNESCO listed the Gelede of Benin, Nigeria and Togo as a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity in 2001. The masks are among the best known in African art museums. See also Oyo.
sum: A masquerade of the Yoruba of southeastern Benin, southwestern Nigeria and Togo, performed to honour and please "our mothers", the elder women and the mystical power they are believed to hold.
